subject: Chemistry
title: Moseley Fixes the Table
description: A quick, practical guide to Moseley Fixes the Table.

hook.text: In 1913, Henry Moseley discovered that the true order of elements is atomic number, not atomic weight.

buildup.text: Mendeleev had ordered elements by weight, but some pairs seemed out of place. Tellurium and iodine didn't fit.

discovery.text: Moseley shot X-rays at elements and found each had a unique frequency tied to its number of protons.

twist.text: Moseley was just 25. A year later, he died at Gallipoli in World War I—a devastating loss for science.

climax.text: His work fixed every misplacement in the table and told chemists exactly how many elements remained to find.

punchline.text: Atomic number, not weight. Moseley perfected the table at 25.

quiz.question: What did Moseley discover about the periodic table?
options: Elements should be ordered by atomic number, not weight
That all elements emit the same X-rays

details.summary: Henry Moseley discovered in 1913 that atomic number, the number of protons in the nucleus, not atomic weight, determines an element's correct position in the periodic table..
details.whyItMatters: Moseley resolved longstanding anomalies where atomic weight ordering disagreed with chemical properties. His work definitively established atomic number as the organizing principle that gives the periodic table its fundamental structure.
takeaways: Moseley proved that atomic number, not weight, determines periodic table position
X-ray spectroscopy revealed each element's unique atomic number fingerprint
His work identified exactly how many elements remained undiscovered

faq.question: What problem did Moseley's discovery solve in the periodic table?
faq.answer: Some elements had their properties in the wrong groups when ordered by atomic weight. For example, tellurium (127.6) has a higher atomic weight than iodine (126.9) but clearly belongs before it based on chemistry..

faq.question: What happened to Moseley after his groundbreaking discovery?
faq.answer: Moseley enlisted in the British Army during World War I and was killed at the Battle of Gallipoli in 1915 at age 27. His death was widely regarded as one of the greatest scientific losses of the war. It prompted the British government to stop assigning prominent scientists to combat duty.
